{"answers":[{"question_id":"Q010_rossmann_family_function_divergence","answer":"SCOPe interprets these as distinct families with probable remote common ancestry, illustrating functional divergence within a shared nucleotide-binding scaffold.

In SCOPe 2.08, the families are alcohol dehydrogenase-like C-terminal domains, c.2.1.1 (SUNID 51736); CoA-binding domains, c.2.1.8 (51900); and potassium-channel NAD-binding domains, c.2.1.9 (63944). All belong to the NAD(P)-binding Rossmann-fold domains superfamily, c.2.1 (51735), within fold c.2 (51734) and the alpha/beta class c (51349). Family membership indicates closer evolutionary relationships; shared superfamily membership supports probable common ancestry despite potentially weak sequence similarity. Fold membership alone establishes similar structural architecture, not necessarily homology, while class describes broad secondary-structure organization.

Their biological roles are not interchangeable. Alcohol-dehydrogenase-like C-terminal domains provide a cofactor-binding component in proteins whose catalytic activity also depends on other regions. CoA-binding domains accommodate CoA in their respective enzyme contexts; inclusion in a superfamily named NAD(P)-binding does not establish NAD(P) specificity or redox activity. Potassium-channel NAD-binding domains place nucleotide binding in a channel-associated context, potentially coupling ligand state to regulation; they should not automatically be assigned alcohol dehydrogenase activity or identified as the ion-conducting pore.

Thus, neither alcohol oxidation, CoA-dependent chemistry, channel regulation, nor exact NAD versus NADP preference should be transferred across these families from SCOPe membership alone. Even a family assignment does not guarantee identical substrates or reactions. Specific functional claims require sequence/profile alignments, conserved binding and catalytic residues, ligand-bound structural evidence, whole-protein domain context, and biochemical or channel-function measurements as appropriate. A cross-family structure may serve as a template for the conserved Rossmann core after alignment, but does not reliably specify binding loops, active-site geometry, domain interfaces, or whole-protein function. Representative selection should therefore match the intended family, domain coverage, and structural quality rather than treating one superfamily member as representative of all three functions.","evidence_used":["Pretrained knowledge of SCOPe hierarchy and protein structure–function interpretation","mcp__scope__get_scop_node","mcp__scope__list_scop_children","/api/v1/releases/current","/api/v1/releases/2.08/sccs/c.2.1","/api/v1/releases/2.08/sccs/c.2.1/parents","/api/v1/releases/2.08/sccs/c.2.1/children?limit=100"]}]}
